proofs.proof_tex:
We first establish the equivalences asserted in the theorem. Reflexivity follows immediately from Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\). For the binary case, write the response table in the order \(0,1\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) becomes
\[
 R_{10}-R_{01}=0,
\]
so every legal binary table satisfies \(R=R^{\mathsf T}\). For an arbitrary table, the map
\[
 T_{ab}\longmapsto T^\dagger_{ba}=R_{ab}-T_{ab}
 \tag{1}
\]
is a bijection from \(\mathcal T_R(h,g)\) to \(\mathcal T_{R^{\mathsf T}}(g,h)\): the row sums of \(T^\dagger\) are the control histogram \(g\), and the column sums of \(R^{\mathsf T}-T^\dagger\) are the treated histogram \(h\). Moreover,
\[
 \prod_{a,b}\binom{R_{ab}}{T_{ab}}
 =\prod_{a,b}\binom{R_{ab}}{R_{ab}-T_{ab}}
 =\prod_{a,b}\binom{R^{\mathsf T}_{ba}}{T^\dagger_{ba}}.
\]
Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) therefore gives
\[
 W_R(h,g)=W_{R^{\mathsf T}}(g,h).
 \tag{2}
\]
When \(K=2\), the equality \(R=R^{\mathsf T}\), (2), and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) imply \(P_R(C)=P_R(C^{\mathsf T})\) for every legal \(R\). Thus \(C\sim C^{\mathsf T}\). For \(K\geq3\), Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}endpoint\text{-}saturation}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) similarly give \(C_+\sim C_-\).

Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}transpose\text{-}reduction}\) shows that an equivalence class contains no profile other than \(C\) and \(C^{\mathsf T}\). It remains to show, when \(K\geq3\), that every nontrivial transpose pair other than \(\{C_+,C_-\}\) is separated by a legal table with at most three heterogeneous units. Fix \(C=(h,g)\neq C^{\mathsf T}\), set \(r=h+g\), and let
\[
 S=\{a\in\mathcal A_K:r_a>0\}.
\]
Suppose first that \(S\) contains an interior level. Join two distinct elements of \(S\) unless they are the pair \(\{0,L\}\). The resulting graph is connected, because any interior vertex is adjacent to every other vertex. If
\[
 h_ag_b-g_ah_b=0
 \tag{3}
\]
on every edge, then \(g=r-h\) turns (3) into \(h_ar_b=r_ah_b\). Hence \(h_a/r_a\) is constant on \(S\). Since Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}profile\text{-}space}\) gives \(\sum_a h_a=m\) and \(\sum_a r_a=2m\), that constant is \(1/2\), whence \(h=g\), a contradiction. Thus there are \(a<b\) in \(S\), with \(\{a,b\}\neq\{0,L\}\), for which (3) is nonzero.

Choose \(u,v\in\mathcal A_K\) by
\[
 (u,v)=
 \begin{cases}
 (b-a,0),&a>0,\\
 (b+1,1),&a=0.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{4}
\]
In the second case \(b<L\), so every value in (4) belongs to \(\mathcal A_K\). In both cases \(a+u=v+b\), and the response types \((a,v)\) and \((u,b)\) are heterogeneous. Define
\[
 R_2=D_{r-e_a-e_b}+E_{av}+E_{ub}.
 \tag{5}
\]
The support conditions \(r_a,r_b>0\) make the diagonal filler nonnegative. The table has mass \(2m\), and its two effects sum to \((a-v)+(u-b)=0\), so Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}table\text{-}mass}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\), through Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}legal\text{-}response\text{-}tables}\), make (5) legal. Its heterogeneous count is two by Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}heterogeneous\text{-}count}\).

The four treatment statuses of the two special units yield pooled special outcomes
\[
 e_a+e_u,qquad e_a+e_b,qquad e_v+e_u,qquad e_v+e_b,
\]
respectively. Direct substitution from (4) shows that only the second equals \(e_a+e_b\). Hence only treating the \((a,v)\) unit and controlling the \((u,b)\) unit can complete the diagonal filler to pooled histogram \(r\). By Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) and the identities
\[
 \binom{s-1}{t-1}=\frac{t}{s}\binom{s}{t},
 \qquad
 \binom{s-1}{t}=\frac{s-t}{s}\binom{s}{t},
\]
whose denominators here are positive, we obtain
\[
 W_{R_2}(C)=Q_r(h)\frac{h_ag_b}{r_ar_b},
 \qquad
 W_{R_2}(C^{\mathsf T})=Q_r(h)\frac{g_ah_b}{r_ar_b}.
 \tag{6}
\]
We used \(Q_r(g)=Q_r(h)\), which follows coordinatewise from \(g_a=r_a-h_a\) and binomial symmetry. Every factor in \(Q_r(h)\) is positive. Thus (3) and (6) separate the two profiles.

It remains to consider a nontrivial transpose pair supported on \(\{0,L\}\). Write
\[
 h_0=m-i,quad h_L=i,qquad g_0=m-j,quad g_L=j,qquad i\neq j.
 \tag{7}
\]
Both \(r_0\) and \(r_L\) are positive; otherwise the two arm-size constraints would force \(h=g\). Because \(L\geq2\), the table
\[
 R'_2=D_{r-e_0-e_L}+E_{L,1}+E_{0,L-1}
 \tag{8}
\]
is nonnegative, has mass \(2m\), and is legal: its two heterogeneous effects are \(L-1\) and \(-(L-1)\). An endpoint-only observed profile is possible only when both special units are treated, since their control outcomes are interior, including when \(L=2\). The same binomial cancellation as above gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 W_{R'_2}(C)-W_{R'_2}(C^{\mathsf T})
 &=\frac{Q_r(h)}{r_0r_L}\{h_0h_L-g_0g_L\}\\
 &=\frac{Q_r(h)}{r_0r_L}(i-j)(m-i-j).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{9}
\]
Thus (8) separates whenever \(i+j\neq m\).

Suppose \(i+j=m\). Then \(r_0=r_L=m\), \(h_0=j\), and \(g_0=i\). If \(i=0\) or \(j=0\), the unordered pair is exactly \(\{C_+,C_-\}\). Otherwise \(i,j>0\); since they are distinct, \(m\geq3\). Define
\[
 R_3=D_{r-2e_0-e_L}+E_{L,0}+E_{0,1}+E_{0,L-1}.
 \tag{10}
\]
The diagonal filler is nonnegative. The three heterogeneous effects sum to
\[
 L-1-(L-1)=0,
\]
so (10) is legal and \(q(R_3)=3\). To yield an endpoint-only profile, the last two special units must be treated because their control outcomes are interior. The first must also be treated: otherwise their pooled observed histogram is \(3e_0\), rather than the missing \(2e_0+e_L\). Thus precisely one special-unit allocation contributes, even for \(L=2\), when the last two response types coincide. Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 W_{R_3}(C)
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{h_0(h_0-1)h_L}{m^2(m-1)},\\
 W_{R_3}(C^{\mathsf T})
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{g_0(g_0-1)g_L}{m^2(m-1)},\\
 W_{R_3}(C)-W_{R_3}(C^{\mathsf T})
 &=Q_r(h)\frac{ij(j-i)}{m^2(m-1)}\neq0.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{11}
\]
All divisions are valid because \(m\geq3\), and the last inequality uses \(i,j>0\) and \(i\neq j\). Equations (6), (9), and (11), together with Lemmas \(\mathrm{lem{:}transpose\text{-}reduction}\) and \(\mathrm{lem{:}endpoint\text{-}saturation}\), prove the complete classification.

We finally verify the uniform separator bound constructively for arbitrary inequivalent \(C=(h,g)\) and \(C'=(h',g')\). If \(h+g\neq h'+g'\), Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}diagonal\text{-}reduction}\) separates them with \(D_{h+g}\), because its count for \(C\) is the positive integer \(Q_{h+g}(h)\) and its count for \(C'\) is zero. If the pooled histograms equal \(r\) but \(Q_r(h)\neq Q_r(h')\), the same diagonal table separates them. Both diagonal separators have \(q=0\).

Suppose the pooled histograms and diagonal coefficients agree. Put \(d=h-g\) and \(d'=h'-g'\). For distinct supported \(a,b\), the symmetric switch
\[
 S_{ab}=D_{r-e_a-e_b}+E_{ab}+E_{ba}
\]
is legal, has \(q(S_{ab})=2\), and direct expansion of its two pooled-compatible special allocations gives
\[
 W_{S_{ab}}(C)=Q_r(h)\frac{h_ah_b+g_ag_b}{r_ar_b}
 =\frac{Q_r(h)}{2r_ar_b}\{r_ar_b+d_ad_b\}.
 \tag{12}
\]
The same formula holds for \(C'\). Suppose all off-diagonal products in (12) agree. If \(d=0\), then \(d'_ad'_b=0\) for every \(a\neq b\), so \(d'\) has at most one nonzero coordinate. The balanced arm-size constraints give \(\sum_a d'_a=0\), hence \(d'=0\). If \(d\neq0\), its zero sum gives at least two nonzero coordinates \(p,q\). Their nonzero product makes \(d'_p,d'_q\) nonzero. For any \(a\notin\{p,q\}\), the equality \(d_pd_a=d'_pd'_a\) shows that \(d_a=0\) if and only if \(d'_a=0\). If there is a third nonzero coordinate \(a\), define \(\lambda_c=d'_c/d_c\) on the common support. Product equality gives
\[
 \lambda_p\lambda_q=\lambda_p\lambda_a=\lambda_q\lambda_a=1,
\]
so \(\lambda_p=\lambda_q=\lambda_a\in\{-1,1\}\); comparison with \(p\) gives the same ratio for every other supported coordinate. If \(p,q\) are the only nonzero coordinates, the zero sums give \(d_q=-d_p\) and \(d'_q=-d'_p\), while \(d_pd_q=d'_pd'_q\) gives \((d'_p)^2=d_p^2\). Thus in every case \(d'=d\) or \(d'=-d\). Since \(h=(r+d)/2\) and \(g=(r-d)/2\), this would make \(C'=C\) or \(C'=C^{\mathsf T}\). Therefore, if \(C'\) is neither, some switch (12) separates with \(q=2\). A remaining inequivalent transpose can occur only for \(K\geq3\) and, by the already proved case analysis, is separated by (5), (8), or (10), with heterogeneous count two, two, or three. Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) now yields \(d(C,C')\leq3\).

Put \(j=m-i\). The profiles in the statement have endpoint coordinates
\[
 h_0=j,quad h_L=i,qquad g_0=i,quad g_L=j,
 \tag{1}
\]
and all interior coordinates vanish. The hypotheses \(1\leq i\leq m-1\) give \(i,j>0\), so the pair is not \(\{C_+,C_-\}\); the hypothesis \(2i\neq m\) gives \(i\neq j\), so the profiles are distinct transposes. Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) therefore proves inequivalence and \(d(C,C')\leq3\). We prove the reverse inequality.

Fix \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) with \(q(R)\leq2\). If \(q(R)=0\), every unit is diagonal. Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}diagonal\text{-}reduction}\) gives zero count for both profiles unless \(R=D_{me_0+me_L}\); for that table, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) and binomial symmetry give
\[
 W_R(C)=\binom mj\binom mi
 =\binom mi\binom mj=W_R(C').
 \tag{2}
\]
The case \(q(R)=1\) is impossible: all diagonal units contribute zero to the weak-null sum, whereas the unique heterogeneous unit contributes a nonzero integer \(a-b\), contradicting Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).

It remains to consider \(q(R)=2\). Label the two heterogeneous units by their response types \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\), with repeated table cells represented by separate labeled units. Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\) says
\[
 a+c=b+d.
 \tag{3}
\]
If any diagonal filler unit has an interior outcome, it is observed at that interior level under every assignment, so both endpoint-only profiles have count zero. We may therefore assume all diagonal filler units lie at \(0\) or \(L\). Partition the labeled assignments according to the four treatment statuses of the two special units.

If both special units are treated and contribute nonzero count, then \(a,c\in\{0,L\}\). They cannot both be zero, since (3) and nonnegativity would imply \(b=d=0\); they cannot both be \(L\), since (3) and \(b,d\leq L\) would imply \(b=d=L\). Either conclusion would contradict heterogeneity. Hence their treated outcomes have multiset \(\{0,L\}\), and a nonzero count requires \(m-1\) diagonal filler units at each endpoint. The filler-selection coefficients for \(C\) and \(C'\) are, respectively,
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j-1}\binom{m-1}{i-1}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i-1}\binom{m-1}{j-1},
 \tag{4}
\]
so they agree. If both special units are controlled, the same argument applied to \(b,d\) gives equal coefficients
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j}\binom{m-1}{i}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i}\binom{m-1}{j}.
 \tag{5}
\]

Now suppose the first special unit is treated and the second is controlled. If either observed outcome \(a,d\) is interior, both contributions vanish. If \(a,d\in\{0,L\}\) are different, then (3) forces both response types to be diagonal. For example, \((a,d)=(0,L)\) gives \(c-b=L\), hence \((c,b)=(L,0)\); the reverse case is symmetric. This contradicts heterogeneity. Therefore a nonzero contribution requires \(a=d=v\) for some \(v\in\{0,L\}\). Equation (3) then gives \(b=c=u\), so the two response types are \((v,u)\) and \((u,v)\), with \(u\neq v\). One special observation of \(v\) lies in each arm. Consequently the diagonal filler contains \(m-2\) units at \(v\) and \(m\) at the opposite endpoint \(\bar v=L-v\). The two coefficients are
\[
 \binom{m-2}{h_v-1}\binom m{h_{\bar v}}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{m-2}{g_v-1}\binom m{g_{\bar v}}.
 \tag{6}
\]
They agree because (1) implies \(h_v+g_v=m\) and \(h_{\bar v}+g_{\bar v}=m\), and hence each binomial coefficient is the complementary one. The other mixed treatment status is identical after exchanging the two labels.

The four cases exhaust every labeled assignment, so (4)--(6) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) imply \(W_R(C)=W_R(C')\) for every legal \(R\) with \(q(R)\leq2\). The positive common normalizer in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) gives equality of the corresponding probabilities. Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) therefore yields \(d(C,C')\geq3\), which with the upper bound proves \(d(C,C')=3\).

For the requested finite early-kill audit, take \(K=3\), \(m=3\), \(L=2\), and \(i=1\). The cubic construction in (10) of the proof of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) is
\[
 R=E_{20}+2E_{01}+E_{00}+2E_{22}.
\]
Its mass is six and its weak-null effect sum is \(2-2=0\). Direct expansion over all \(\binom63=20\) balanced assignments gives count \(1\) for \(C=((2,0,1),(1,0,2))\) and count \(0\) for \(C'=C^{\mathsf T}\). Independently enumerating the nonnegative \(3\times3\) integer tables of mass six, imposing the weak-null equation and \(q(R)\leq2\), leaves \(103\) tables; the exhaustive four-status argument above gives equal counts for this pair for every one. This computation is a check of, and not a premise for, the all-size proof.

For a bijection \(f\) of \(\mathcal X_{m,K}\), Definitions \(\mathrm{def{:}maximal\text{-}common\text{-}group}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\) give
\[
 f\in G_\star
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 f(C)\sim C\ \text{for every }C\in\mathcal X_{m,K}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Thus every such \(f\) maps each equivalence class into itself. Since the profile space is finite and \(f\) is bijective, its restriction to each class is a permutation. Conversely, any independently chosen permutation within each equivalence class preserves every \(P_R\) by Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}probability\text{-}equivalence}\), and hence belongs to \(G_\star\). Composition and inversion act classwise. Therefore
\[
 G_\star\cong\prod_{A\in\mathcal X_{m,K}/\sim}S_A.
 \tag{2}
\]

When \(K=2\), each arm histogram is determined by its number of ones, so \(|\mathcal X_{m,2}|=(m+1)^2\). Exactly \(m+1\) profiles have identical treated and control histograms and hence are fixed by transposition. Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) says all other equivalence classes are two-point transpose classes. Their number is
\[
 \frac{(m+1)^2-(m+1)}2
 =\frac{m(m+1)}2
 =\binom{m+1}{2}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The singleton factors in (2) are trivial, so (3) yields
\[
 G_\star\cong(S_2)^{\binom{m+1}{2}}.
\]
When \(K\geq3\), Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) gives exactly one two-point class, \(\{C_+,C_-\}\), and singleton classes otherwise. Equation (2) then gives \(G_\star\cong S_2\), whose only nonidentity action exchanges those two endpoint corners.

Fix \(G\leq G_\star\), a statistic \(T\), and a profile \(C\). Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}maximal\text{-}common\text{-}group}\) shows that every \(G\)-orbit has one or two points. If the orbit of \(C\) is a singleton, every \(f\in G\) fixes \(C\), and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}orbit\text{-}rank\text{-}pvalue}\) gives \(p_G(C)=1\).

Suppose the orbit is \(\{C,C^*\}\). Choose \(f_*\in G\) with \(f_*(C)=C^*\). Left multiplication by \(f_*\) is a bijection between the group elements that fix \(C\) and those that send \(C\) to \(C^*\). Thus exactly \(|G|/2\) elements have each image. Since \(T(C)\geq T(C)\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}orbit\text{-}rank\text{-}pvalue}\) yields
\[
 p_G(C)=
 \begin{cases}
 1/2,&T(C^*)<T(C),\\
 1,&T(C^*)\geq T(C).
 \end{cases}
 \tag{1}
\]
Hence \(p_G(C)\in\{1/2,1\}\) in every case, including the trivial subgroup.

Now fix \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\). By Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}maximal\text{-}common\text{-}group}\),
\[
 P_R(f(C))=P_R(C)\qquad(f\in G).
 \tag{2}
\]
Therefore, conditional on any positive-probability \(G\)-orbit, the observed profile is uniform on that orbit. If \(0\leq\alpha<1/2\), (1) makes the rejection event empty. If \(1/2\leq\alpha<1\), a singleton orbit contributes no rejection. On a two-point orbit, at most the point with strictly larger \(T\)-value rejects, because two real numbers cannot each be strictly larger than the other; by (2), that point has conditional probability \(1/2\). Summing over the disjoint positive-probability orbits gives
\[
 \Pr_R\{p_G(C)\leq\alpha\}\leq\frac12\leq\alpha.
 \tag{3}
\]
For \(\alpha=1\), the event is the whole profile space and has probability one. These cases prove finite-sample validity for every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}balanced\text{-}complete\text{-}randomization}\) and Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) identify \(P_R\) in (2) with the actual assignment-induced profile law, so (3) is the asserted design-based probability statement.

added_lemmas.statement:
Under the hypotheses and notation of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}unbalanced\text{-}frontier}\), for every \(G\leq G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}\), every \(T:\mathcal X_{n_1,n_0,K}\to\mathbb R\), and every \(C\in\mathcal X_{n_1,n_0,K}\), the conventional nonrandomized orbit-rank value
\[
 |G|^{-1}\bigl|\{f\in G:T(f(C))\geq T(C)\}\bigr|
\]
is identically \(1\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex: Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}unbalanced\text{-}frontier}\) proves \(G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}=\{\operatorname{id}\}\). Therefore every subgroup \(G\leq G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}\) is \(\{\operatorname{id}\}\), so \(|G|=1\), its orbit of every \(C\) is the singleton \(\{C\}\), and \(T(\operatorname{id}(C))=T(C)\). Substitution into the displayed rank formula gives \(1^{-1}|\{\operatorname{id}\}|=1\).
added_lemmas.justification: This is the unequal-allocation half of the orbit-rank elbow: singleton all-schedule equivalence classes force the conventional common-group procedure to be completely degenerate.
added_lemmas.gap: The balanced rank calculation alone does not state the consequence of the exact unequal-arm singleton theorem.
added_lemmas.consumer: For design-audit software, this distinguishes the balanced two-point-orbit limitation from the identity-only common group under every unequal allocation.

prose_updates.tldr: Exact weak-null symmetry has an allocation-balance elbow. Under balanced complete randomization, binary outcomes retain precisely the arm-transpose classes, whereas alphabets with \(K\geq3\) retain only the opposing endpoint-corner pair; for \(K\geq3\) and \(m\geq3\), the worst-case legal separator needs exactly three heterogeneous units. Every unequal complete-randomization allocation has only singleton classes, identity maximal common group, and optimal worst-case separator complexity two. Consequently conventional nonrandomized common-orbit ranks lie in \(\{1/2,1\}\) when balanced and are identically \(1\) when unequal. An explicit non-orbit exact p-value prevents any broader impossibility interpretation.

project_justification.gap: Weak-null randomization theory supplies asymptotic studentization or exact inversion over compatible schedules, while general permutation theory begins with a specified invariant group. It does not compute how the probability-equivalence partition of all fixed zero-average-effect schedules changes exactly at equal versus unequal arm allocation.
project_justification.niche: For a finite outcome alphabet, fixed potential-outcome schedules and complete randomization produce an exact multivariate-hypergeometric coefficient system. Computing its common stabilizer exposes allocation balance, rather than alphabet size alone, as the decisive symmetry boundary.
project_justification.fill: The paper classifies the balanced and unequal-arm equivalence partitions, derives their maximal common bijection groups, and certifies the optimal worst-case sparse-separator complexities: three in the nonbinary balanced frontier and two for every unequal allocation. It then derives the corresponding conventional orbit-rank granularity while retaining a constructive non-orbit exact counterexample to any general impossibility claim.

sampling_model.design: Complete randomization with a fixed treated count \(n_1\) and control count \(n_0=n-n_1\). The balanced case \(n_1=n_0=m\) and every unequal case \(n_1\neq n_0\) are analyzed separately.
sampling_model.treatment: Exactly \(n_1\) units receive treatment and \(n_0\) receive control; balance means \(n_1=n_0=m\).
sampling_model.overlap: Every labeled assignment with the prescribed treated count has the same positive probability \(\binom{n}{n_1}^{-1}\), specialized to \(\binom{2m}{m}^{-1}\) under balance.

prose_updates.related_work: \cite{WuDing2021} frames the weak-null obstacle through missing potential outcomes and obtains asymptotic control by studentization. \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} supplies orbit-counting validity once a finite invariant group is given; here the group is computed from the full composite causal null. \cite{DutzZhang2026} concerns invariant bijections for i.i.d. finite-support product laws. The present paper instead conditions on a fixed potential-outcome schedule and studies assignment-induced multivariate-hypergeometric laws. Neither model class is used as a subclass of the other, and no converse or invariance classification is transferred between them. \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} and \cite{LiDing2016} obtain exact binary average-effect confidence sets through compatible-table reasoning rather than a common group, while \cite{AronowChangLopatto2025} gives a balanced computational acceleration for that inversion problem. \cite{ChungRomano2013} studies unequal group proportions through asymptotic multinomial--hypergeometric coupling; the unequal-allocation result here is an exact fixed-schedule coefficient classification. \cite{ZhaoDing2021} supplies the robustly studentized weak-null workflow motivating the applied audit, but its weak-null guarantee is asymptotic rather than the common-invariance statement studied here.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The general cubic identity and the lower bound against every legal schedule with at most two heterogeneous units are proved analytically by expanding the special-unit treatment statuses. The \(K=3,n=6\) enumeration, which gives cubic counts \(1\) and \(0\) and checks all \(103\) legal tables with \(q(R)\leq2\), is only a diagnostic stress test. Separator complexity counts heterogeneous units, not enumeration time or statistical power. The exact group result also does not justify replacing the HC2 or robust-\(t\) weak-null workflow, whose guarantee and objective are different.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The results concern fixed no-interference schedules, complete randomization with positive fixed arm sizes, histogram-measurable common bijections, and equally spaced finite alphabets. They cover both balanced and unequal allocations: the balanced partition has the stated transpose or endpoint-corner classes, whereas every unequal partition is singleton. The separator lower bound of three is asserted only for \(K\geq3\) and \(m\geq3\); the unequal worst-case value two holds over its stated admissible range. The orbit-rank conclusion applies only to conventional nonrandomized ranks generated by a schedule-universal group. It does not classify every exact weak-null test, validate a particular sharp-null permutation statistic, or cover covariate-adaptive, stratified, or clustered designs.

statement_notes.justification: This theorem supplies the balanced side of the allocation-balance elbow and an explicit legal separator with at most three heterogeneous units for every inequivalent profile pair.
statement_notes.gap: The i.i.d. finite-support product-law criterion of \cite{DutzZhang2026} and the asymptotic fixed-population result of \cite{WuDing2021} do not classify this all-schedule assignment-induced hypergeometric kernel.
statement_notes.consumer: DeclareDesign's balanced \(250\)-of-\(500\) binary reply audit can use the exact transpose classification to distinguish a justified histogram symmetry from a sharp-null imputation or an asymptotic HC2 argument.

statement_notes.justification: This theorem certifies that three heterogeneous units are genuinely necessary in the worst nonbinary balanced case, rather than an artifact of the cubic construction.
statement_notes.gap: Neither exact binary test inversion in \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} nor generic group testing in \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} studies the optimal sparse legal-schedule certificate number.
statement_notes.consumer: It fixes the smallest worst-case adversarial schedule size that a balanced nonbinary symmetry classifier must include in a software audit.

statement_notes.justification: This translates the balanced probability partition into the largest schedule-universal transformation group; paired with the unequal frontier, it isolates identity as the exact off-balance group.
statement_notes.gap: \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} proves validity for a specified invariant group, whereas the new step is computing the maximal group forced by the composite causal null and showing its discontinuous change with allocation balance.
statement_notes.consumer: It supplies an allocation-specific validation target for software advertised as a weak-null common-invariance randomization test.

statement_notes.justification: This theorem gives the balanced inferential consequence of maximal common symmetry; Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}unbalanced\text{-}orbit\text{-}rank\text{-}degeneracy}\) supplies the unequal-arm corollary \(p_G\equiv1\).
statement_notes.gap: The rank argument is elementary once the group is known; the substantive new input is the exact orbit-size elbow derived from the fixed-schedule coefficient kernel.
statement_notes.consumer: For the binary reply audit, the result explains why conventional common-orbit ranks cannot reproduce a \(5\%\) HC2 or robust-\(t\) workflow, while making no claim against nuisance-aware or otherwise non-orbit exact tests.

statement_notes.justification: This records the requested unequal-arm consequence of the identity maximal common group.
statement_notes.gap: Without this corollary, the orbit-rank narrative would stop at the balanced \(\{1/2,1\}\) granularity despite the discharged unequal-arm classification.
statement_notes.consumer: It tells design-audit software that changing only the arm allocation from equal to unequal removes even the nontrivial common orbit.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(C=(h,g)\) and \(C'=(h',g')\), and use the convention \(\binom uv=0\) unless \(0\leq v\leq u\).  We first verify the coefficient formula from the randomization design.  For a fixed response table \(R\), a treated-count matrix \(T\) specifies that exactly \(T_{ab}\) of the \(R_{ab}\) labeled units of type \((a,b)\) are treated.  There are
\[
 \prod_{a,b\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{R_{ab}}{T_{ab}}
\]
such assignments.  The row constraints on \(T\) give the treated histogram \(h\), and the column constraints on \(R-T\) give the control histogram \(g\).  Distinct matrices \(T\) describe disjoint assignments.  Summing over \(\mathcal T_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)\) therefore gives \(W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)\).  Complete randomization assigns probability \(\binom n{n_1}^{-1}\) to each assignment, and \(\binom n{n_1}>0\) because \(1\leq n_1\leq n-1\).  Division gives the displayed formula for \(P_R^{(n_1)}\).

For \(r\in\mathbb Z_+^K\) satisfying \(\sum_a r_a=n\), let \(D(r)\) be the diagonal table with \(D(r)_{aa}=r_a\).  It has mass \(n\) by the displayed condition on \(r\), and every unit has individual effect zero.  Thus the finite-population normalization and the weak-null condition imply \(D(r)\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).  Directly from the coefficient formula,
\[
 W_{D(r)}^{(n_1)}(u,v)
 =\mathbf 1\{u+v=r\}\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\binom{r_a}{u_a}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Set \(r=h+g\) and \(Q_r(h)=\prod_a\binom{r_a}{h_a}\).  Each factor in \(Q_r(h)\) is positive because \(0\leq h_a\leq r_a\).  If \(C\sim_{n_1,n_0}C'\), applying the definition of equivalence to \(D(r)\) and using (1) first yields \(h'+g'=r\), because the count of \(C\) is positive, and then yields
\[
 Q_r(h)=Q_r(h').
 \tag{2}
\]

We next extract the off-diagonal entries of the arm-imbalance outer product using legal two-unit switches.  If \(a\neq b\) and \(r_a,r_b>0\), define
\[
 R^{ab}=D(r-e_a-e_b)+E_{ab}+E_{ba}.
 \tag{3}
\]
The entries of the diagonal filler are nonnegative.  The table in (3) has mass \(n\), while its two heterogeneous effects sum to \((a-b)+(b-a)=0\); hence it belongs to \(\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) and \(q(R^{ab})=2\).  The two special units contribute pooled observed histogram \(e_a+e_b\) when both are treated or both are controlled, \(2e_a\) when the \((a,b)\) unit alone is treated, and \(2e_b\) under the other mixed allocation.  Since the diagonal filler has pooled histogram \(r-e_a-e_b\), precisely the both-treated and both-controlled cases can realize a profile with pooled histogram \(r\).  The identities
\[
 \binom{s-1}{t-1}=\frac ts\binom st,
 \qquad
 \binom{s-1}{t}=\frac{s-t}{s}\binom st
\]
apply with positive denominators \(s=r_a,r_b\), and give
\[
 W_{R^{ab}}^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =Q_r(h)\frac{h_ah_b+g_ag_b}{r_ar_b}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Define
\[
 d=h-g=2h-r,
 \qquad
 d'=h'-g'=2h'-r.
\]
Because
\[
 h_ah_b+g_ag_b=\frac{r_ar_b+d_ad_b}{2},
 \tag{5}
\]
equivalence, (2), and (4) imply
\[
 d_ad_b=d'_ad'_b
 \quad\text{whenever }a\neq b\text{ and }r_a,r_b>0.
 \tag{6}
\]

The diagonal entries of the same outer product follow from a second switch placement.  Fix \(a\) with \(r_a\geq2\), choose \(b\neq a\), which is possible because \(K\geq2\), and put
\[
 \widetilde R^{a\mid b}=D(r-2e_a)+E_{ab}+E_{ba}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Again the table has mass \(n\), its two nonzero effects cancel, and \(q(\widetilde R^{a\mid b})=2\).  The diagonal filler has pooled histogram \(r-2e_a\).  Exactly one allocation of the special units supplies the missing pooled histogram \(2e_a\): the \((a,b)\) unit is treated and the \((b,a)\) unit is controlled.  The other three allocations supply either \(e_a+e_b\) or \(2e_b\), which differ from \(2e_a\) because \(a\neq b\).  Therefore
\[
 W_{\widetilde R^{a\mid b}}^{(n_1)}(h,g)
 =\prod_c\binom{r_c-2\mathbf 1\{c=a\}}
                       {h_c-\mathbf 1\{c=a\}}
 =Q_r(h)\frac{h_ag_a}{r_a(r_a-1)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
The last division is valid because \(r_a\geq2\).  Equivalence and (2) now imply \(h_ag_a=h'_ag'_a\), whence
\[
 d_a^2=r_a^2-4h_ag_a
      =r_a^2-4h'_ag'_a=(d'_a)^2.
 \tag{9}
\]
If \(r_a=0\), both imbalance coordinates are zero.  If \(r_a=1\), integrality and \(h_a,h'_a\in\{0,1\}\) give \(d_a^2=(d'_a)^2=1\).  Thus (9) holds for every \(a\).  Together with (6), including the trivial products involving a zero-support coordinate, this proves
\[
 dd^{\mathsf T}=d'(d')^{\mathsf T}.
 \tag{10}
\]

The unequal allocation is used at exactly this point.  The two profile constraints give
\[
 \sum_a d_a=\sum_a d'_a=n_1-n_0=: \delta\neq0.
 \tag{11}
\]
In particular, \(d\neq0\).  Choose \(j\) with \(d_j\neq0\).  The \((j,j)\) entry of (10) gives \(d'_j=\varepsilon d_j\) for some \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), and every \((j,a)\) entry then gives \(d'_a=\varepsilon d_a\).  Summing and applying (11) gives \(\delta=\varepsilon\delta\); since \(\delta\neq0\), necessarily \(\varepsilon=1\).  Hence \(d'=d\), and therefore
\[
 h'=\frac{r+d'}2=\frac{r+d}2=h,
 \qquad
 g'=\frac{r-d'}2=\frac{r-d}2=g.
\]
Thus every equivalence class is a singleton.

The preceding proof gives an explicit separator for every distinct pair.  If the pooled histograms differ, the table \(D(h+g)\) has a positive count for \(C\) and count zero for \(C'\) by (1).  If the pooled histograms agree but the two values of \(Q_r\) differ, the same diagonal table separates them.  Suppose instead that (2) holds.  If an off-diagonal product in (6) differs, the table (3) separates the profiles by (4).  If all those products agree but the profiles are distinct, some squared coordinate in (9) must differ: otherwise (10)--(11) would imply \(C=C'\).  Such a coordinate must have \(r_a\geq2\), because squared imbalance is forced to be zero when \(r_a=0\) and one when \(r_a=1\); the table (7) then separates the profiles by (8).  Every constructed table is legal and has at most two heterogeneous units.  Consequently
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)\leq2.
 \tag{12}
\]
Moreover, if \(f\in G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}\), then the defining probability identity says \(C\sim_{n_1,n_0}f(C)\) for every \(C\).  Singleton equivalence classes force \(f(C)=C\) for every \(C\), so \(G_\star^{(n_1,n_0)}=\{\operatorname{id}\}\).

It remains to prove that the uniform bound in (12) is sharp.  Because \(n=2m\), positive unequal arm sizes cannot occur when \(m=1\), so here \(m\geq2\).  Define
\[
 \ell=\max\{0,n_1-m\},
 \qquad
 u=\min\{m,n_1\}.
\]
The inequalities \(1\leq n_1\leq2m-1\) imply \(\ell<u\), and splitting into the cases \(n_1\leq m\) and \(n_1>m\) gives \(\ell+u=n_1\).  Using the levels \(0,1\in\mathcal A_K\), define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 h&=\ell e_0+u e_1,
 &g&=(m-\ell)e_0+(m-u)e_1,\\
 h'&=u e_0+\ell e_1,
 &g'&=(m-u)e_0+(m-\ell)e_1.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{13}
\]
The entries are nonnegative, the arm sizes are \((n_1,n_0)\), both profiles have pooled histogram \(r=me_0+me_1\), and they are distinct because \(\ell<u\).  A response table with \(q(R)=0\) is diagonal.  Formula (1) makes both counts zero unless \(R=D(r)\), while for \(R=D(r)\),
\[
 W_R^{(n_1)}(h,g)=\binom m\ell\binom mu
 =\binom mu\binom m\ell
 =W_R^{(n_1)}(h',g').
 \tag{14}
\]
There is no legal response table with \(q(R)=1\): diagonal units contribute zero to the weak-null sum, whereas the unique heterogeneous unit would contribute \(a-b\neq0\), contradicting the weak-null condition.  Hence the pair (13) cannot be separated by fewer than two heterogeneous units.  Combining this lower bound with (12) proves
\[
 s_\star(n_1,n_0,K)=2.
\]

For the smallest admissible instance \((n,K,n_1,n_0)=(4,2,1,3)\), (13) gives \((h,g)=((0,1),(2,1))\) and \((h',g')=((1,0),(1,2))\).  Under \(D(2e_0+2e_1)\), both assignment counts equal \(2\), and under every other diagonal table both counts vanish.  The legal table \(2E_{11}+E_{01}+E_{10}\), which is (7) with \(a=0\) and \(b=1\), gives counts \(0\) and \(1\), respectively, by the direct coefficient calculation in (8).  This exact boundary enumeration verifies both the two-unit construction and the obstruction to a separator with fewer heterogeneous units.

Let \(B=\binom{2m}{m}\).  Since \(m\geq 1\), \(B\) is a positive integer.  Fix \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\).  By the balanced complete-randomization assumption and the definition of the exact randomization kernel, every balanced assignment has probability \(B^{-1}\), and hence
\[
 \Pr_R\{C=C_+\}=P_R(C_+)=B^{-1}W_R(C_+).
\]
The endpoint-saturation lemma gives \(W_R(C_+)\in\{0,1\}\), so
\[
 \Pr_R\{C=C_+\}\leq B^{-1}. \tag{1}
\]
By the definition of \(p_{\mathrm{corner}}\),
\[
 p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)=
 \begin{cases}
 B^{-1},&C=C_+,\\
 1,&C\neq C_+.
 \end{cases} \tag{2}
\]
Let \(\alpha\in[0,1]\).  If \(0\leq\alpha<B^{-1}\), equation (2) makes the rejection event empty, and therefore its probability is zero.  If \(B^{-1}\leq\alpha<1\), equation (2) gives
\[
 \{p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)\leq\alpha\}=\{C=C_+\};
\]
consequently (1) yields
\[
 \Pr_R\{p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)\leq\alpha\}
 \leq B^{-1}\leq\alpha.
\]
Finally, if \(\alpha=1\), the rejection event is the entire profile space and has probability \(1=\alpha\).  These cases exhaust \([0,1]\), proving exact validity for every legal response table.

Equation (2) also shows that the unique value of \(p_{\mathrm{corner}}\) below one is \(B^{-1}=\binom{2m}{m}^{-1}\).  For \(m=1\) it equals \(1/2\).  For every \(m\geq2\),
\[
 B=\binom{2m}{m}\geq\binom{4}{2}=6,
\]
where the inequality follows because \(\binom{2(m+1)}{m+1}/\binom{2m}{m}=2(2m+1)/(m+1)>1\).  Thus \(B^{-1}<1/2\) whenever \(m\geq2\), establishing the asserted possibility without imposing any restriction on other exact tests.

proposed.statement: For every \(K\geq2\), the function \(p_{\mathrm{corner}}\) satisfies \(\Pr_R\{p_{\mathrm{corner}}(C)\leq\alpha\}\leq\alpha\) for every \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) and every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\). Its nontrivial value is \(\binom{2m}{m}^{-1}\), which can be strictly below \(1/2\).
proposed.justification: This analytic counterpoint prevents the group classification from being misread as nonexistence of all other exact weak-null tests.
proposed.gap: Exact binary procedures in \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} already show that nuisance-aware tests can exist; this proposition isolates a particularly transparent non-orbit rule inside the present model.
proposed.consumer: It tells DeclareDesign developers that an exact weak-null module may use analytic calibration or nuisance maximization even though common-orbit ranks are coarse.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The exact randomization-kernel definition is a direct premise of the displayed probability calculation and is therefore added to the declared proof spine.
